newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar firm, rise to 127 yen stymied in late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar firm, rise to 127 yen stymied in late Tokyo.

text.p: 0626 GMT 2400 GMT NYK CLOSE

The dollar was firmer but stalled below earlier highs in late Tokyo Wednesday trade, with a try for 127 yen blocked for now by profit-taking and options-linked sales. It briefly touched 1.7200 marks before backing off.
Earlier, driven by aggressive buying from U.S. funds and securities firms, the greenback rose as far as 126.93 yen, its highest level since August 1992.

These operators, who bought most actively in morning trade, were joined later in the day by Japanese interbank operators. "Bank traders took heart from the morning gains and began buying in the afternoon," one trust bank dealer said.

But the greenback soon stalled and spent much of the afternoon stuck between 126.70 and 126.90 yen, gradually drifting lower. This prompted some profit-taking from operators who had bought earlier and were disappointed in the greenback's failure to break above 127 yen, a U.S. bank dealer said.
Many in the market also said that sales linked to knockout options at 127 yen flat were likely near 126.95 yen.
"As things go right now, without fresh factors, there's no question that a lot of people are interested in selling near 126.95 yen," one dealer said.
But few believed this weakness would last. "Overall, there is still no change in the overall bullish dollar mood," another U.S. bank dealer said, citing the dollar's gains on the mark.

Technical factors also hinted at further rises. The dollar had managed to break through one resistance point at 126.75 yen, but a city bank dealer said the next technical resistances were not seen until 127.40 and then 128.00 yen. Other dealers said there were no major resistances up until 128.20 yen.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in early afternoon that Japan would maintain its current easy credit policy, as the Bank of Japan had made clear, but this had no impact.

"This should be a dollar-buying factor, but there have been so many different and confusing comments from Japanese government officials recently that the market has started to become desensitised to them," one U.S. bank dealer said.

On his way back to Washington from Asia, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin denied suggestions that he and Japanese officials had discussed trying to cap the dollar's rise during their discussions in Tokyo last week.
"If they (the Japanese) are (trying to do that), they didn't discuss it with us," Rubin said. He added that he had accomplished what he wanted in the meetings.
This briefly boosted the dollar in the mid-afternoon, but it soon fell back again in the face of profit-taking.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, said in an interview published in Wednesday's Yomiuri Shimbun that Japan's long-term interest rates were at record-low levels, reflecting a market view that the economy had been in bad shape for a considerable time.

"However, once people realise that the Japanese economy is not that bad, long-term interest rates will rise, causing a plunge in bond prices and thus forcing people who are now buying bonds to incur losses," he said. This comment pushed Japanese market interest rates up and temporarily dragged the dollar down against the yen in morning trade.
The dollar briefly hit 1.7200 marks, and dealers said there was more room for it to rise here than against the yen.
Singapore dealers said the dollar was in strong demand with Japanese banks seen bidding actively on any dips. -Singapore newsroom (65-8703080), E. Lies in Tokyo +81-3-3432-8806
